name: Kastor-Traschen Colliding Black Holes
description: Any number of charged black holes in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, the exact solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations David Kastor and Jennie Traschen found in 1993. Each hole has a charge equal to its mass, and the holes ride the expansion or the contraction of the universe, so holes that fall together merge.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. Each hole carries the mass parameter $m_i = GM_i/c^2$, a length, and a charge $Q_i$ of one common sign with $GQ_i^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4) = m_i^2$. The cosmological constant is $\Lambda = 3H^2/c^2$.
history: Give a point mass an electric charge equal to its mass, set a second one beside it, and the pair stays wherever you put it: in Newton's theory the electric repulsion cancels the gravitational attraction at every separation [kastor1993]. General relativity keeps that balance exactly, for any number of such charges at rest: Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Achilles Papapetrou each found the solution in 1947 [majumdar1947, papapetrou1947]. James Hartle and Stephen Hawking showed that every one of those point charges is a black hole, its point a horizon of area $4\pi m_i^2$ [hartle1972]. What becomes of the standoff when the universe around the holes expands?¶A positive cosmological constant $\Lambda$ changes what a charge equal to the mass means [kastor1993]. In de Sitter space the hole with $|Q| = M$ is the one whose horizon is exactly as hot as the cosmological horizon around it, the hole Larry Romans named "lukewarm", and the extremal hole carries more charge than mass [mellor1989, romans1992, kastor1993]. David Kastor and Jennie Traschen asked how a test particle with charge equal to its mass moves near such a hole [kastor1993]. With the least energy its areal radius grows or shrinks at the rate $c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$ times itself, as it would in empty de Sitter space, so that the particle "is, in some sense, not affected by the presence of the $Q = M$ black hole" [kastor1993]. That was their hint to promote the test particles to black holes [kastor1993].¶In coordinates that ride the expansion, that one hole is Majumdar and Papapetrou's with a scale factor $a = e^{Ht}$ put in, $H = \pm c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, and the same substitution gives any number of holes, $$ds^2 = -\frac{c^2dt^2}{\Omega^2} + a^2\Omega^2\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\right), \qquad \Omega = 1 + \sum_i \frac{m_i}{a|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|}$$ [kastor1993]. Each hole keeps its place $\mathbf{x}_i$ and the universe does the moving [kastor1993]. With $H < 0$ the holes fall together and merge, and $H > 0$ is the time reverse [kastor1993, brill1994]. In their words, "Black holes merge, and white holes split" [kastor1993]. To their knowledge it was "the first analytic description of coalescing black holes" [kastor1993]. At $\Lambda = 0$ the solution is Majumdar and Papapetrou's again [kastor1993].¶Is there a largest black hole? With $\Lambda > 0$ there is: as the mass parameter $m$ of the $|Q| = M$ hole grows, its horizon closes on the cosmological horizon, the two meet at $m = c/(4|H|)$, and a heavier hole leaves its singularity naked [brill1994]. What if two holes, each lighter than that limit and together heavier, collide? Tetsuya Shiromizu, Ken-ichi Nakao, Hideo Kodama, and Kei-ichi Maeda had argued, with no exact solution to hand, that black holes of large area cannot collide in de Sitter space unless a naked singularity forms [shiromizu1993, brill1994]. Dieter Brill, Gary Horowitz, Kastor, and Traschen ran the collision in the exact solution, written in the time $\tau$ with $H\tau = e^{Ht}$ as $ds^2 = -c^2d\tau^2/U^2 + U^2\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\right)$, $U = H\tau + \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$, which runs on past $\tau = 0$ to the singularity $U = 0$ [brill1994]. Below the limit the holes coalesce, the event horizon one sphere around each hole at early times and a single surface around both later, and above it a naked singularity forms to the future of a Cauchy horizon [brill1994].¶The horizons of several holes are rougher than one hole's [brill1994]. Across the cosmological horizon the metric is twice differentiable and in general not smooth, and across the inner horizon of each hole it is once differentiable, with a curvature singularity mild enough that geodesics pass through it [brill1994]. One hole alone is smooth everywhere, and Brill and his coauthors read the roughness as electromagnetic and gravitational radiation in the spacetime besides the holes [brill1994]. The solution fixes where the holes are and how heavy, but neither their velocities nor that radiation, so they wrote that "we cannot yet claim that this is a serious violation of cosmic censorship" [brill1994]. Miguel Zilhão, Vitor Cardoso, Leonardo Gualtieri, Carlos Herdeiro, Ulrich Sperhake, and Helvi Witek collided uncharged black holes in de Sitter space on a computer and found that pairs of large total mass lose causal contact even when they start close together, as cosmic censorship asks [zilhao2012].¶How do two horizons become one? Nakao, Shiromizu, and Sean Hayward followed two equal holes numerically: below the critical total mass a new trapping horizon, the edge of a region that light cannot leave, appears around both of the original ones [nakao1995]. Daisuke Ida, Nakao, Masaru Siino, and Hayward traced the event horizon by its light rays: it is a pair of trousers, and the points where new rays join it form a spacelike seam of finite length [ida1998]. They called this spacetime "at present the only such analytic solution" of colliding black holes [ida1998]. These holes may be the lightest things that can carry their charge: any number of them admit supercovariantly constant spinors, which Kastor and Traschen took as a sign of a state of least energy [kastor1996]. Gary Gibbons and Maeda found an exact relative, maximally charged black holes in a universe that expands with an arbitrary equation of state, a solution with a scalar field and two Maxwell fields [gibbons2010].

related.text: These holes with the cosmological constant switched off. At $H = 0$ the time drops out of the metric and the holes stand still [kastor1993].
One hole alone is the lukewarm charged black hole in de Sitter space, the one as hot as its cosmological horizon, in coordinates that ride the expansion [kastor1993, brill1994].
The universe the holes ride in. With every mass set to zero the metric is de Sitter space in its flat slicing [kastor1993].
A mass in an expanding universe filled with fluid, where the pressure piles up around the mass to keep the density even [kastor1993].

Two uncharged black holes at rest in a universe with no cosmological constant. Only their first moment is in closed form, and the collision that follows is known from computer simulations [brill1963, sperhake2015].
